column1: Pricing the maximum POI import over the accounting period is correct for today's Leistungspreis and is about to stop being the only regime that matters.
Under §19(2) S.1 StromNEV, atypische Netznutzung, the charge is based on the peak within published Hochlastzeitfenster rather than the annual maximum.
HLZF windows are published per DSO per year.
Under §19(2) S.1 the optimisation target is a max over a subset of slots defined by a data table.
Under §19(2) S.2 StromNEV, stromintensive Netznutzung, qualification requires at least 7,000 full-load hours and more than 10 GWh annual consumption at the metering point, with tiered reductions.
Full-load hours are annual energy divided by annual peak power.
Battery operation moves both the numerator and the denominator of full-load hours and therefore moves §19(2) S.2 qualification directly.
§19(2) S.2 qualification is a cliff: falling below 7,000 full-load hours loses the reduction for the entire year.
A myopic optimiser that shaves a peak in December can raise full-load hours and gain, while one that discharges to capture a spread can lower annual consumption and lose far more than the spread.
The qualification cliff is a discrete state with a large terminal value and belongs in the value function rather than in the per-tick objective.
ITariffRegime is a plug-in interface, and PeakView selects a regime from configuration and emits shapes accordingly.
The AnnualLeistungspreis regime emits an EpigraphTerm over all slots in the year, floored by the realised peak, and is today's baseline.
The MonthlyLeistungspreis regime emits an EpigraphTerm per calendar month.
The AtypicalHlzf regime emits an EpigraphTerm over HLZF slots only, taken from the calendar table.
The IntensiveUse regime emits an EpigraphTerm plus a discrete qualification state.
Tariff regimes compose, and a site can be subject to more than one simultaneously, such as an HLZF-based charge and a volumetric charge.
Each regime emits terms tagged with its own EconomicEffect, so the composer's exclusivity check keeps them from overlapping.
Qualification state is a state variable in L0 and a dimension of V.
qualState carries accumulated annual energy, accumulated full-load hours, current HLZF exposure and a projected qualification probability.
The value function is fitted conditional on the discrete qualification state, which is how the cliff is represented without breaking concavity in SOC.
Cliff protection is a hard guard and not only an economic term.
When projected qualification is within a configurable margin of a threshold, the engine raises a peakCritical or qualCritical flag.
The peakCritical or qualCritical flag forces escalation to a higher co-optimisation tier and applies a bound restricting actions that would worsen the projection.
Losing a year of network-charge reduction for a day's spread is the single largest downside event in the BTM business case and must not be reachable through an approximation error.
A regime change is a configuration date plus a new regime implementation, not a rewrite.
Backtests spanning a regime change are honest, because the regime is selected from the versioned calendar.
All numeric tariff thresholds — 7,000 hours, 10 GWh, tier percentages, HLZF windows — are configuration sourced from the current published tables per DSO and per year, never constants.
Regulation in the area of individual network charges is actively moving.
Hardcoding max over the month cannot express HLZF and silently mis-prices the qualification cliff.
Treating qualification as a post-hoc report guarantees the engine will eventually trade through a cliff for a small gain.
The execution engine already exists and is fixed, so the question the engine must answer at C3 is which limit orders, at what price and what volume, to submit.
A MILP answers what net position is wanted in each slot, which is a different question from what limit orders to submit.
Turning a target position into a limit price is a separate problem involving fill probability, urgency, adverse selection and the shape of the remaining trading window.
Limit price is not naturally a MILP variable, because price is a control on a stochastic fill process rather than a physical quantity.
Conflating position and quoting either gives the MILP price variables and non-convexities it cannot handle, or buries the quoting logic inside the optimiser where it cannot be tested or tuned.
The Planner decides the target position per slot and per market, with a shadow value of position change — the marginal EUR/MWh at which the engine is indifferent.
The Planner emits an urgency signal derived from how much the objective degrades if the position is not reached.
The Quoting Policy maps target, shadow value, urgency, FillProbView and market microstructure state to a ladder of limit orders with price, volume, validity and replace/cancel behaviour.
The shadow value is the Planner's own indifference price, which gives the quoting policy an economically meaningful bound.
The quoting policy must never quote a price worse than the shadow value, because at that price the trade destroys value.
Everything between the current market and the shadow value is the region the quoting policy is free to work in, and its job is to capture as much of that spread as fill probability allows.
C3 carries intent and not routing.
An OrderIntent is (market, product, slot, side, limitPrice, volume, validity, replacesId, tag) and says nothing about venue mechanics.
The Execution adapter translates intent into whatever the simulator or a live venue requires.
To the Planner, fill probability crosses C2 as a BoundTerm limiting how much volume may be counted on, carrying no price.
The fill-probability BoundTerm prevents the Planner from planning on volume it will not get.
To the quoting policy the full fill-probability curve P(fill | price, time-to-gate) is available, because that is precisely the trade-off it exists to make.
Because Execution is fixed, the fill model is calibrated against the simulator's actual behaviour and re-verified whenever the simulator changes.

T4 includes a quoting-policy backtest that measures realised fill rate against predicted fill rate by price band, and systematic divergence is a calibration failure that is reported rather than absorbed.
The Planner stays a clean MILP over physical quantities, with no price variables and no fill-probability non-convexity inside the solver.

The quoting policy can be replaced, A/B tested and tuned independently with the Planner held fixed, so its contribution to P&L is separately measurable as the execution slippage bucket in Settlement's four-way decomposition.
The DA case requires a bid curve rather than a single quantity.
The Planner produces the DA bid curve by parametric re-solve across a grid of DA clearing prices, yielding a monotone price-quantity schedule.
Monotonicity of the DA bid curve is required by exchange rules and by economic sense, and is asserted.
A non-monotone DA bid curve indicates a formulation error, most often a missing coupling constraint.
Splitting intent from quoting costs an extra component, and the shadow value must actually be extracted from the solve rather than approximated.
Price as a MILP variable introduces the fill process into the solver and makes it non-convex and unstable.
A fixed offset from mid ignores the shadow value entirely and will trade through indifference under pressure.
Quoting inside Execution is rejected because Execution is strategy-independent by design and quoting is strategy.
The system's entire feedback loop depends on being able to re-run and compare.
A pipeline that produces slightly different answers on re-run cannot be improved, only argued about.

Non-determinism creeps in from solver thread counts and time limits, hash-order iteration, floating-point reduction order under parallelism, wall-clock reads, un-pinned model artefacts, un-pinned tzdata, and data revisions arriving between runs.
Every artefact is content-addressed and every run is reproducible from a manifest.

A run is defined by a manifest containing the hash of the code revision, the configuration, the market calendar artefact, the tzdata version, every model artefact, the data snapshot boundary, the solver identity and version, and the solver determinism settings.
Two runs with the same manifest must produce byte-identical outputs.
Byte-identity under an identical manifest is tested, not asserted.
The solver runs with a fixed seed, a fixed thread count, and a fixed time limit expressed in deterministic work units where the backend supports it, never in wall clock.
Where a backend cannot be made deterministic under parallelism, the reproducibility run uses single-threaded mode and the production run records its non-determinism explicitly.
No component reads the system clock, and time enters through the tick's SlotId and asOf, both supplied by the driver.
A clock read in a layer is a defect enforced by an analyzer rule.
There is no runtime randomness, and scenario draws are artefacts generated offline with a recorded seed.
No code path that affects output iterates over an unordered collection, and ordered keys are used everywhere.
Parallel floating-point reductions use a fixed partitioning scheme so summation order is stable.
BeliefSnapshot, ValuationBundle, PlanResult, StateSnapshot and SettlementResult each carry a content hash of their own contents plus the hashes of their inputs.
The input-and-content hashing gives a Merkle chain over the whole tick.
If a downstream artefact differs between runs, the Merkle chain localises which upstream input diverged.
Because every contract is a serialisable value type, each seam can be recorded to disk during a run.
A recorded seam is a test fixture: Valuation can be replayed against a recorded C1 stream with no Belief store present, and the Planner against a recorded C2 stream with no Valuation present.
Seam recording is what makes per-layer golden tests possible and is the reason the contracts carry no object references.
Regression testing is a hash comparison, so refactors are safe to attempt because they are cheap to verify.
Any behavioural change must be intentional and shows up as a diff in a named artefact, with the Merkle chain pointing at the cause.
The lookahead audit is only meaningful because runs are deterministic, since otherwise a changed result proves nothing.
Recorded seams for a long backtest are large, so the policy is to record seams on demand for designated audit days and to record only hashes for bulk runs.
Determinism costs real discipline, particularly around solver settings and parallelism.
A measured throughput loss is accepted in the reproducibility configuration, while production runs with more threads and records that it is a different manifest.
Approximate reproducibility removes the ability to detect small regressions, which are the ones that matter.
Timestamps as identifiers are not content-addressed: two different runs at the same time are indistinguishable and the same run twice is distinguishable, which is exactly backwards.
